title: Add workflow for auto build and deployment of book
description:
This PR is the last one about deploying our books automatically. 

* ~It uses **renv** to manage packages and install them in the same state as local build~ Edit: it does not anymore - it uses a DESCRIPTION file.
  * I removed some packages installation from index.Rmd. A lot of package where missing installation anyway.
* workflow works the same as other books
	* It uses Makefile to build the book: 
	  * Only Gitbook version on PR to check it builds correctly
	  * Gitbook and PDF (version with strip content) on commit to main
    * It will publish on bookdown.org directly using **rsconnect** package (only on push to main)
      *  I have set up the ID and key in environment secret inside the repo, so it should work.

I am still unsure if it is best to use **renv** or DESCRIPTION + **pak**. The laster have the advantage to autoinstall sys dep on linux, and allows several explicit ways to provides dependency (like book deps for R chunks in Imports, packages required for creating reference with `write_bib()` in Suggests, package for deployement in `Config/need/deploy` for example). But the former have the advantage to lock versions (which could also be an inconvenient.)

Anyway, let's see if that build this way. If you prefere not to use **renv**, I'll make the switch to DESCRIPTION.

title: Create LICENSE
description:
You only specifiy the license of the book's content (CC-BY-SA 4.0) in the [preface](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/) of the book. This first confused me a lot: After submitting a PR and transferring copyright of it to the book's authors I was wondering if the book was actually open source.

Besides allowing visitors of the repository to immediately determine the license of the project (without having to look at the book's preface), specifying the license in a separate file has the advantage of being machine-readable and thus being auto-detected by GitHub (as well as external entities).

I copied the license text 1:1 from [here](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/legalcode.txt).

title: properly document the `output_yaml` option
description:
[rmarkdown 1.16](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown/releases/tag/v1.16) introduced the `output_yaml` metadata option which allows to explicitly specify the path to the external output options file. This wasn't documented in the book up until now. Besides the documentation wasn't (IMHO) clear enough that you can only outsource _output_ options.

_I assign the copyright of this contribution to the authors of the book "R Markdown: The Definitive Guide"._

title: Chapters 16 & 17: templates and new formats
description:
Chapters complete (I hope). I have looked through your edits to my previous PRs and tried to reduce the number of changes you will need to make, but I am sure there are still some stylistic issues you will want to change.

I really wanted to write a lot more about creating custom pandoc templates, but feel this is a complex topic and requires an understanding of LaTeX and HTML. So I have included a single example to at least show how we can use pandoc variables in a template. This is a subject I would like to expand in the "Mastering R Markdown" book though, as I think it is really powerful.

I have also made a few example templates and contained them within a repository: https://github.com/mikey-harper/example-rmd-templates . I wasn't sure whether you wanted me to keep them as part of the book, but if you do like the idea I will expand the description and include a README.md in the repository.

Let me know if there are other things I can help out with on the book for now :) I was going to read through it all and pick out any typos and see if I had any other suggestions.

title: Bookdown draft
description:
Hi @yihui ,

Here is my draft attempt at the book chapter. It is still slightly rough around the edges, but thought it would be best to get some feedback from you before going too far down the wrong route.

**Comments**
- Most the content is taken from the bookdown book but has required a lot of editing to squeeze it down. Generally, I have tried to cut out advanced concepts with the aim of providing details which are sufficient for users to get up and running.
- I have tried my hardest to match your writing style where I have written new content.
- I have added a short section on the typical project files: I think this a nice way of quickly explaining how all the parts link, and is something I remember wanting when I started learning bookdown.
- I generally have provided cross-references to the bookdown book where more detail is provided about advanced concepts. I have tried not to do this too often as it is important that this is lives up to the name and is a definitive guide for most users though.
- I have started preparing cross-references to other parts of the book which are currently missing (Figures, customization)
- I have still yet to write the `Some tips` section, but I think it would be good to end the chapter with some practical tips on usage.

**General questions:**

- [ ]  Can you let me know any improvements I can make to emulate your writing style?
- [ ] I still feel it is slightly too long, so would like to know your thoughts on the overall length.
- [ ] Do you think there are any key topics which I should not have removed?

**Next steps**:
- Shorten the content from `Editing` onwards: I didn't have time to fully cut this down from the book.

Thanks in advance for any help!

title: Update 12-bookdown.Rmd
description:
# Chapter Outline
The aim of this is to capture my overall thoughts and propose an outline for the chapter layout.

## General Comments
### Shortening Process
The general aim is to condense the bookdown book (119 pages) into a single chapter within the RMarkdown book. Basic savings can be made:

-	Markdown syntax (25 pages): this is already covered in Chapter 
-	Appendices (16 pages)

This brings down the number of pages to around 78 page. About 10% of the content can be kept to bring the work down to the required length. How is it best to achieve this reduction and convert the book?

-  Reduce the number of concepts explained?
-  Reduce the detail of concepts explained?

I feel there will clearly be a balance between these two approaches to reduce the amount of content included (as proposed in outline).

### Relationship to bookdown book

Is this RMarkdown book aiming to replace or supplement the bookdown book? If it is aiming to supplement, can cross-references to the bookdown book be made? For example:

>	For more details on the customisation of the `_bookdown.yml`, see chapter X for extra details.

I feel it should be a guidepost, aiming to provide the reader with enough knowledge to get up and running, but also informing them of where to find out more information to achieve the more complex aspects.

### Differences in scope

The bookdown book was presented as a standalone document. Being a chapter of the full book, there is an opportunity for the writing to a new audience who had no necessarily even used Rmarkdown before.

Being part of the book, this chapter serves a slightly different purpose. The reader will know about Rmarkdown, but may need to understand the benefits that bookdown provide for long-form documents and some of the enhancements that it brings for bigger documents.
